text: Both AWS and Azure describe cloud security the exact same way, even if the wording differs slightly: a shared responsibility model. The provider is responsible for security OF the cloud. The customer is responsible for security IN the cloud. That one split explains almost every real-world cloud security incident you'll ever read about, so it's worth understanding precisely where that line actually falls.

Security OF the cloud means the physical datacenter, the host hardware, the hypervisor that isolates one customer's workloads from every other customer's, and the network backbone connecting it all together — that's always the provider's job, no matter which service model you're using. Security IN the cloud means your data, your identity and access management, the network controls you're given to configure, and, whenever you're managing a virtual machine's own operating system, keeping that operating system patched and current.

That line isn't fixed in place — it moves as you climb from IaaS toward SaaS. On a plain EC2 instance, you patch the guest OS and configure its security group yourself, while AWS only secures the physical hardware and the hypervisor beneath it. On a managed database like RDS, AWS patches the OS and the database engine for you, and you just manage the schema, the data, and exactly who gets access to it. On Microsoft 365, Microsoft manages the entire application and its underlying OS, but you still manage every user identity, every sharing setting, and your organization's own data.

This is exactly why a publicly exposed S3 bucket is the customer's fault, not AWS's — access control over your own data is security IN the cloud. A flaw that let one tenant's virtual machine read another tenant's memory through the hypervisor, on the other hand, would squarely be AWS's fault. And in the real world, the overwhelming majority of reported cloud breaches trace back to the customer side of that line: a leaked access key, an overly permissive IAM policy, a storage bucket left wide open — not a failure in the provider's own physical or hypervisor-level security.
